claims.claim: Workers digging a well hit a stone man (the giant was found by well diggers).
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: The figure was ten feet long.
claims.quote: The length of the giant was 10 feet 4+1⁄2 inches (3.162 m)

claims.claim: It lay in a pit behind a barn.
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell

claims.claim: The photograph of the giant is credited to Bain News Service, 1910, public domain.
claims.quote:
Date: 1910
Author: Bain News Service, publisher
Licence: Public domain

claims.claim: The giant was carved in Chicago.
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter. Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant.

claims.claim: George Hull had the giant shaped after his own body.
claims.quote: The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: A geologist told Hull hair would not petrify, so the figure has no hair or beard.
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: The lithograph shown is by Popular Graphic Arts and is titled "The Onondaga Giant".
claims.quote: THE ONONDAGA GIANT.

claims.claim: The block came from an Iowa gypsum quarry.
claims.quote: This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: Hull and H. B. Martin hired men at Fort Dodge in 1868 to quarry the block, telling them it was for a Lincoln monument.
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York.

claims.claim: The block measured ten feet four and a half inches long.
claims.quote: hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: The stereocard image is "View in Cardiff Glen," near Fort Dodge, Iowa, dated 1873, held by the New York Public Library.
claims.quote: VIEW IN CARDIFF GLEN. NEAR FORT DODGE.IOWA.

claims.claim: The back of the stereocard names the hoaxers as George Hull and H. B. Martin.
claims.quote: Their names were George Hull and H. B. Martin.

claims.claim: The card's printed text says the block was taken to Chicago, the giant carved, then shipped to New York and buried in a barn lot.
claims.quote: The block was taken to Chicago, the "Giant" carved, and then shipped to the point in New York which gave it its name, where it was buried in a barn lot, and subsequently "discovered".

claims.claim: Pores were punched into the surface with steel knitting needles embedded in a board.
claims.quote: The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores.

claims.claim: Sand, water and sulphuric acid were used to age the giant.
claims.quote: Hull first wiped the giant using a sponge soaked with sand and water. ... The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: Yale's Othniel Marsh noted fresh tool marks on soluble gypsum and called it "a most decided humbug."
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue, pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did), and termed it "a most decided humbug".

claims.claim: Hull confessed in December 1869 and a court ruled both giants fakes.
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press, and on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court

claims.claim: Whether the Chicago stonecutter knew what he was making remains unclear.
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions, it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving

claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant was not real; it was carved from a block of gypsum in 1868.
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: Two men hired to dig a well behind William Newell's barn uncovered the giant on October 16, 1869.
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant.

claims.claim: Newell put a tent over the giant and charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing.
claims.quote: The next day, a tent was set up on the discovery site and Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant.

claims.claim: Three to five hundred people came per day.
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day

claims.claim: George Hull was a New York tobacconist.
claims.quote: The giant was the creation of a New York tobacconist named George Hull.

claims.claim: Hull lost an argument at a Methodist revival meeting about the giants of Genesis 6:4.
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: Two sculptors in Chicago carved the block.
claims.quote: Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant.

claims.claim: Geologist John F. Boynton said it was not a fossilized man and hypothesized a Jesuit carving.
claims.quote: John F. Boynton, the first geologist to examine the giant, declared that it could not be a fossilized man, but hypothesized that it was a statue that was carved by a French Jesuit in the 16th or 17th century

claims.claim: Andrew D. White of Cornell noted there was no reason to dig a well on that spot.
claims.quote: He noticed that there was no good reason to try to dig a well in the exact spot the giant had been found.

claims.claim: In February 1870 a court declared both Hull's giant and P. T. Barnum's plaster copy fakes.
claims.quote: on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court; the judge also ruled that Barnum could not be sued for terming a fake giant a fake

claims.claim: Barnum's copy was a plaster copy modelled covertly in wax.
claims.quote: he hired a man to model the giant's shape covertly in wax and create a plaster copy

claims.claim: Edward Burkhardt was the Chicago stonecutter.
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter.

claims.claim: The copy in a Michigan arcade museum is called Barnum's only on the say-so of its owner.
claims.quote: The owner of Marvin's Marvelous Mechanical Museum, a coin-operated game arcade and museum of oddities in Farmington Hills, Michigan, has said that the copy displayed there is Barnum's.

claims.claim: The giant was photographed by Bain News Service in 1910.
claims.quote: Author: Bain News Service, publisher
